scenes.name: DJ Kool Herc y el nacimiento del hip hop
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Clive Campbell llegó de Kingston a finales de los sesenta con el recuerdo de los sound systems y los toasters del reggae; grafitero con el tag Kool Herc, el 11 de agosto de 1973 pinchó en la fiesta de vuelta al cole de su hermana Cindy, en el 1520 de Sedgwick Avenue: el nacimiento del hip hop. Con su «Merry-Go-Round» aislaba y alargaba los breaks de los discos alternando dos platos, y los b-boys ya no tenían que esperar a que acabara la canción para bailar. Coke La Rock, un buscavidas con labia, fue el primer MC, gritando nombres sobre la cámara de eco. Su lista de breaks (James Brown, el «Apache» de la Incredible Bongo Band, Baby Huey, Dennis Coffey) era la que tocaban todos; tapaba las etiquetas para que nadie supiera qué era. «Era disco, pero disco de gueto.» De los parques pasó a clubes como el Hevalo (1975).

scenes.name: Hip hop neoyorquino
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Con la música negra popular muerta estéticamente, el alma del pueblo pasó al underground: un funk ruidoso, áspero y tenso, demasiado desesperado para la radio negra. Los breaks de DJ Kool Herc en las fiestas de barrio del Bronx, Jazzy Jay, Afrika Bambaataa, DJ Hollywood, Grandmaster Flash y Eddie Cheeba convirtieron la mezcla de discos en arte: los chavales dejaron las bandas por dos platos, el scratch y los breaks repetidos, un collage posmoderno de toda la música grabada sobre un ritmo funky. Sylvia Robinson grabó en 1979 «Rapper’s Delight» de la Sugarhill Gang y fichó a Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five, cuya «The Message» (1982), con Melle Mel, dio voz a los sin voz como no se oía desde «What’s Going On»; siguieron «White Lines» o «New York, New York». Las cajas de ritmos dieron un funk industrial y minimalista (el bombo 808, «Five Minutes of Funk» de Whodini), y Run-D.M.C. («It’s Like That», «Rock Box», «King of Rock», «Walk This Way» con Aerosmith en Raising Hell, 1986) asaltó la radio rock, seguidos por los Beastie Boys.

podcast.title: Apache and the Perfect Beat
podcast.body: In his 2005 interview with Terry Gross, DJ Kool Herk recounted how his "merry go round" experiment took off with the song "Apache," often referred to as "The Incredible Bongo Rock." He noticed that people would specifically wait for this part of his set. The success of using "Apache" in this manner led other DJs to search for the "perfect beat," though, according to Herk, no one has ever truly beaten "that record" (Apache). "Everybody would come and really wait for that particular part of my format for me to get into it. And that's when everybody started searching for the perfect beat, trying to beat that record."

podcast.title: Father of Hip Hop
podcast.body: Clive Campbell, known as DJ Kool Herk, is widely regarded as the father of hip hop. Born in Jamaica, he moved to New York and began his DJ career by playing at his sister's birthday party. He quickly gained recognition for his skills at house parties and block parties before transitioning to club DJing. "Clive Campbell, a native of Jamaica moved to New York. He is considered by many people to be the father of hip hop."

podcast.title: Origin of Hip-Hop
podcast.body: Hip-hop's existence was traced back to DJ Kool Herc's "legendary 1973 wrap room party," which is cited as the starting point of the genre, over a decade before its significant pop culture infiltration in 1984. "By 84, hip-hop had existed for over a decade since DJ Kool Herk's legendary 1973 wrap room party."

podcast.title: The Merry Go Round Technique
podcast.body: DJ Kool Herk pioneered the "merry go round" technique, which involved using two turntables to extend the "break" sections of funk and soul records. He observed that dancers (B-boys) would wait for specific parts of records to perform their special moves. By extending these instrumental breaks, he allowed dancers more time to "do their thing" and showcase their best moves, which became known as breakdancing in the 1980s. He discussed this experiment in a 2005 interview with Terry Gross on NPR's Fresh Air. "He took that to turn table technique to extend the break like the ones we just heard and give it up or turn it a loose, which he called the merry go round."
